name: Body wraps

lead: Body wraps give a quickly slimmer-looking waist and lower tape measurement, which people use before an event or photo. The inch loss is visible right away.

The torso or limbs are wrapped in bandages, plastic or neoprene, sometimes after mud or lotion, and sometimes with a sauna suit. Heat and compression cause sweating and temporary water loss and may compress tissue. The FDA has stated that wraps cause temporary water loss rather than fat loss and that the fluid is quickly replaced. Proponents also claim toning, skin firming and toxin removal; reference sources cite no clinical studies for those claims.

paras: Users wrap up for a session at a spa or at home, then measure afterward, timing it close to the occasion since the effect fades as they rehydrate. Some combine wraps with lotions or mud treatments.

The FDA warns that rapid, excessive fluid loss can cause severe dehydration and electrolyte imbalance. Tight wraps and heat add further strain, so people with heart or kidney conditions and those who are heat-sensitive generally avoid them.

web.title: Body Wraps to Lose Weight - Healthline

chain: Slimmer measurements for a short time
angle.text: Wraps and sauna suits give a quickly slimmer-looking waist or a lower tape measurement before an event. The inch loss is visible right away; per the FDA, it is water that returns, and fat loss from wraps is not shown.

lead: Body wraps are spa and home treatments in which the torso, waist or limbs are wrapped in bandages, plastic film or neoprene, often after mud, herbal preparations or lotions are applied, and sometimes combined with a PVC sauna suit. People use them to look slimmer and smoother for a short time, for example before an event or photo, because measurements and the look of the skin can change after a session.[1][2]

Healthline reports that wraps are marketed for losing inches, dropping weight and tightening loose skin, with most sessions lasting 30 to 90 minutes and the skin rinsed and moisturized afterwards.[2] Spa options described there include heat wraps, slimming wraps with lotions or herbal products, infrared wraps and 'detoxing' wraps, while neoprene wraps are said to raise core temperature and induce sweating.[2]

Proponents also say wraps hydrate and firm skin, relax muscles and help the body 'flush out toxins'.[1] The US Food and Drug Administration, as summarized by Wikipedia, has stated that inches or pounds lost during a wrap come from sweating and are temporary because the fluid is replaced by drinking and eating.[1] Healthline makes a similar point and adds that the skin may look and feel smoother afterward.[2]

Published medical research on 'body wraps' covers other uses: therapeutic wet and dry sheet wraps used in psychiatry, skin-to-skin wraps in neonatal care, burn dressings and plastic wraps for keeping surgical patients warm.[3][4][5][6][7] Sauna suits, the sweat-inducing garments that overlap with wraps, have a documented history in combat sports and have been restricted in school and college athletics.[8]

paras: In a typical spa treatment, mud or another preparation is applied to the skin and the area is covered with bandages, sometimes inside a plastic or PVC suit, to induce sweating.[1] Consumer versions include neoprene waist wraps and sauna suits worn during exercise.[2]

Healthline lists several spa formats: heat wraps, slimming wraps applied with lotions or herbal products, infrared wraps and detoxing wraps said to draw toxins from the skin.[2] It also describes do-it-yourself wraps sold by private sellers, often containing mud, clay, herbs or creams, which typically call for exfoliating first and stay on for 30 to 90 minutes, with neoprene wraps sometimes worn longer.[2]

A sauna suit is a waterproof garment, historically rubber or rubberized cloth and now usually PVC or coated nylon, with elastic at the waist, neck, wrists and ankles that traps heat and moisture so the wearer sweats heavily during exercise.[8] Wrestlers and other weight-class athletes have used them to lose water weight quickly, often together with restricted eating and drinking.[8]

Wikipedia's account of the suits is mostly about that sporting history: it reports that the National Federation of State High School Associations banned sauna suits in 1977, that the NCAA banned them in 2013, that several collegiate wrestlers died of hyperthermia in 1997 while on rapid weight-cutting regimens, and that a 2022 British Journal of Sports Medicine study found higher in-competition injury risk among Division I wrestlers who cut weight by perspiration-induced dehydration.[8] Wellness-style neoprene belts and waist wraps are a lighter consumer version of the same idea.[2]

Wrap marketers say heat and compression make the body sweat, tighten the look of the skin and reduce measurements, with claims ranging from a few pounds and inches in one session to several dress sizes over repeated treatments.[2] Wikipedia describes proponents as saying wraps slim, tone, hydrate and firm the body and help with sore muscles and joint inflammation.[1]

Healthline also lists reduced cellulite and toning of loose skin among the marketed claims, and notes that users often combine wraps with other weight-loss methods, which makes it hard to attribute any change to the wrap itself.[2]

For appearance, the practical draw is speed. The measurable change after a session is a smaller tape-measure reading or a flatter, smoother-feeling surface for a short time, which is why wraps are often scheduled before an event, a photoshoot or a weigh-in.[2] Spa wraps with lotions or mud also leave the skin exfoliated and moisturized, which users describe as a smoother, more even surface.[1][2]

The FDA position summarized by Wikipedia is that any weight lost is from fluid and is quickly regained, that wraps do not affect fat deposits, and that fat is reduced when calorie intake falls below energy expenditure.[1] Healthline reports that most supporting evidence comes from companies that sell wraps and that little unbiased research exists; it adds that skin may look tighter afterward but often only for a short time.[2] Its sources for the discussion include FDA consumer guidance on weight-loss products and a systematic review of diet and exercise treatments.[2]

The FDA warning cited by Wikipedia states that rapid, excessive fluid loss can cause severe dehydration and electrolyte imbalance.[1] Healthline lists dehydration, overheating, discomfort from tight compression, wearing a wrap longer than intended and unknown reactions to herbal, exfoliating or moisturizing ingredients as risks, and notes that dehydration risk rises when wraps are worn during exercise.[2]

The sources Wikipedia cites for the FDA warning are a 1982 FDA Consumer article by Judith Willis and a 2009 ABC News report titled 'Body Wraps Come with Strings Attached'.[1] The sporting literature on sauna suits describes heat illness among athletes who combined them with fluid restriction.[8]
No studies found on cosmetic slimming wraps. Medical literature on 'body wraps' concerns other uses.

A randomized feasibility trial of therapeutic wet and dry sheet wraps enrolled 48 children with autism and severe injurious behaviour and found irritability scores improved in both groups with no difference between them.[3] An observational study of 26 healthy volunteers who experienced tightly wrapped wet cold sheets plus warm blankets, compared with 13 resting controls, reported lower heart and breath rates and lower salivary cortisol, which its authors read as an anxiolytic effect.[4] A pilot of 29 parent-preterm infant pairs found that using a body wrap to hold infants for skin-to-skin care did not significantly change hold time, adverse events or parental stress.[5] A randomized trial of two plastic wraps during major surgery compared heat retention between a reflective and a standard wrap.[6] A retrospective cohort study described therapeutic wraps used on Swiss adult psychiatric wards.[7]

lore.intro: Wraps are promoted by spas and wrap brands and covered by health media, mostly for short-term inch loss before events.[2]
